catalog_quote: As is typical in Mon-Khmer languages, well-formed words in Lavïa can be monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic, or a compound comprising elements exemplifying either syllable type. In sesquisyllabic words, a phonologically reduced minor syllable precedes a stressed major syllable. The iambic stress pattern also carries over to compound words, although the first compound element is not phonologically reduced; e.g. kuan ʔiá ‘chick’; lai muóʔ ‘time’; vu vɨɒ́ʔ ‘get dark’; lu lié ‘swim around’. ... Seven minor syllables occur in our data: ʔa-, pa-, ka-, ca-, la-, ra-, and si-. Minor syllables are unstressed with indistinctly pronounced vowels.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are monosyllables, sesquisyllables or compounds of these. Stress falls on the major (last) syllable: in a sesquisyllable the reduced minor syllable (ʔa-, pa-, ka-, ca-, la-, ra-, si-) is unstressed and the following major syllable is stressed; in two-element compounds the second element carries the stress (iambic), even though the first element is a full, unreduced syllable. Effectively fixed word-final stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Minor-syllable vowels are 'realized with fully articulated vowels in citation or deliberate speech only' (p. 287). The language has no contrastive tone or phonation (pp. 286, 306-307).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (sesquisyllabic words and compound words); citation-form remark concerns minor-syllable vowel realization. Description is of the Banzhe (班哲) village variety, Mengka Town, Ximeng County, from first-hand data collected in Kunming.
new_statements.identity_note: Sun 2020 describes the Lavïa (Masan 马散 / la-vɨɒʔ) variety of Banzhe village, Mengka Town, Ximeng County -- the 'Lavia' component of Glottolog's Lavia-Awalai-Damangnuo Awa (awac1238, ISO vwa). Sun (p. 286, n. 3) argues Lavïa is a distinct Wa-Lawa language and that Awalai and Damangnuo 'may also turn out to be separate languages'; the Xiyun subdialect (Va, tonal, monosyllabic; Sun 2018) is excluded from the awac1238 name and is a different phonological type. The stress statement should be taken as describing Banzhe Lavïa; Sun (n. 24) extends only the absence of tone/register, not the stress remark, to the Masan, Zhongke, Yuesong and Yancheng varieties.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables (reduced minor syllable + major syllable); stress falls on the major syllable, i.e. the last syllable of the word (iambic). In compounds the same iambic pattern holds: the final element carries the stress (marked with an acute on the second element in the examples), even though the first element is not reduced. No contrastive tone or phonation/register in Banzhe Lavïa; footnote 24 extends the tonelessness to the Masan, Zhongke, Yuesong and Yancheng varieties reported in Zhou et al. (2004).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. Minor syllables are explicitly unstressed with indistinct vowels (fully articulated only in citation or deliberate speech).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Sun notes (p. 306) that Drage (1907) apparently heard multiple tones in the Lavïa dialect(s) he worked on and asks whether this reflects an earlier tonal or phonation stage in some Lavïa dialects; no exception to the iambic stress placement is given.
new_statements.identity_note: Sun 2020 describes the Banzhe (pa-cʰək) Village variety, Mengka Town, Ximeng County, Yunnan, which Sun equates with the Chinese-source 'Awa' Masan-type Lavïa; the Awalai and Damangnuo varieties grouped under the same Glottolog languoid are treated by Sun as distinct Wa-Lawa languages (n. 3) and are not described. Drage 1907 (not opened) describes an unspecified Lavïa/Wa variety in Burma per Sun.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement among the sources actually opened: only Sun 2020 was readable, and it agrees with the catalog (iambic stress on the major/final syllable, no tone or register). A latent, second-hand tension exists on tone rather than stress: Sun 2020 (p. 306) reports that Drage 1907 apparently transcribed multiple tones for an unspecified Lavïa variety, whereas Sun finds Banzhe (and, per n. 24, Masan, Zhongke, Yuesong, Yancheng) to have no contrastive tone or phonation; Sun attributes this either to Drage's 'shaky transcription' or to an earlier tonal/phonation stage in some dialects. Drage 1907 itself could not be opened (Google Books 403 captcha twice; not on archive.org; HathiTrust catalog 403), so this could not be checked. The Academia.edu preprint (Sun 2018b) could not be opened either (an automated-access block on both attempts).

sources.note: Describes standard (Parauk/Aishuai) Wa only; p. 8 (Chapter 1): the Ximeng/Menglian dialects 'referred to in Chinese as Awa.. are not represented in this study.' No word-stress rule for Awa; for standard Wa it only notes sesquisyllabic /s./ presyllables (sec. 4.2.1) and an 'emphatic high tone' on the last syllable of an utterance 'or even any stressed word' (Ch. 6).
